content: The guidelines for managing latent tuberculosis infection, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2015, do not express any opinion regarding the legal status of any country, territory, city, or area, nor do they address the delimitation of borders. Any dotted or dashed lines on maps included in the publication represent approximate boundaries, which may not have full agreement. The mention of specific companies or products does not imply endorsement or preference by WHO over other similar products not mentioned. Proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information in this publication. However, the material is distributed without any warranty, expressed or implied. The responsibility for interpreting and using the material lies with the reader, and WHO is not liable for any damages arising from its use. The guidelines cover topics such as latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI), immunologic tests, Mycobacterium tuberculosis immunology, antitubercular agents, and related recommendations. The publication includes acknowledgments, abbreviations, conflict of interest declarations, an executive summary, evidence quality and recommendation strength, preventive treatment for contacts of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) cases, program management, monitoring, evaluation, references, and annexes. The development and drafting of the guidelines were coordinated by Haileyesus Getahun and Alberto Matteelli under the direction of Mario Raviglione. The WHO Steering Group included experts from various departments, such as the Global TB Programme and the HIV/AIDS Department. The guidelines development group was co-chaired by Holger Schünemann (McMaster University, Canada) and Jay Varma (US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention). Holger Schünemann also served as the GRADE methodologist. The guidelines development group included a diverse range of experts from institutions worldwide, such as the University College London, the Ministry of Health in Brazil, the Karolinska Institute in Sweden, and the University of Indonesia, among others. These members contributed their expertise in LTBI, TB control, and related fields. Systematic reviews were conducted by consultants and organizations, including Pallas Health Research and Consultancy BV and Public Health England. All contributors completed a WHO Declaration of Interest form, and potential financial conflicts of interest were evaluated by members of the Steering Group. Intellectual conflicts of interest were not considered grounds for exclusion, as broader expertise on LTBI was deemed essential. The diversity and representation within the group were sufficient to balance and address any potential intellectual conflicts. The guidelines were financially supported by the Ministry of Health of Italy, with additional funding from core WHO funds. Public Health England supported systematic reviews on the predictive utility of tuberculin skin tests (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) and on the best treatment options for LTBI. The guidelines also reference studies funded by the UK Department of Health, including randomized controlled trials comparing isoniazid-rifapentine and isoniazid-rifampicin for LTBI treatment. The guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based recommendations and the use of systematic reviews and meta-analyses to inform decision-making. They aim to provide comprehensive guidance for the management of LTBI, including preventive treatment, program management, and evaluation strategies.
